title: Business Management HL · Set B · Paper 2
subject: business-management

questions.title: Section A · Bracken Sensors
questions.stem: Bracken assembles monitoring units. Normal annual capacity is 50,000 units and output is 40,000. Total annual fixed manufacturing overhead is CU 360,000. Each unit sells for CU 48 and uses CU 28 in variable costs. A one-off foreign order for 8,000 units offers CU 35 per unit. Shipping the order would cost CU 16,000 in total. Normal sales can be maintained.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate current capacity utilization and fixed manufacturing overhead per unit if fixed overhead is allocated over actual output.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the change in operating profit if Bracken accepts the order.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why an absorption-costing appraisal and a contribution appraisal could lead to different decisions.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain one reason spare capacity measured annually might overstate Bracken’s ability to fulfil this order.

steps.text: Divide current output by normal capacity.
Allocate CU 360,000 over 40,000 units.
CU 9 per unit.
Incremental contribution before freight is 8,000 × (35 − 28).
Net gain is CU 40,000 after shipping.
The allocated production cost of CU 37 per unit exceeds the offered price of CU 35.
At spare capacity, allocated fixed costs remain payable with either decision.
Contribution focuses on the extra revenue and avoidable costs of this order.
Normal sales and the order might peak in the same weeks.
Overtime, outsourcing or late delivery could reduce the calculated gain.

questions.title: Section A · Mora Studio
questions.stem: Mora has non-current liabilities of CU 240,000 and equity of CU 360,000, with no other long-term capital. It earns annual profit before interest and tax of CU 84,000. A project needs CU 150,000 and is forecast to add CU 15,000 to annual profit before interest and tax. It can be financed by new long-term debt or ordinary shares. Annual interest on the new debt would be 8%.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate current gearing and return on capital employed. Use non-current liabilities as a percentage of capital employed for gearing.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate gearing after expansion under each financing option.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate additional annual profit before tax after interest if Mora borrows. Explain one implication for risk.

steps.text: Capital employed is CU 600,000.
Gearing is 40%.
Divide CU 84,000 by CU 600,000 and multiply by 100.
ROCE is 14%.
Capital employed is CU 750,000 in either case.
Interest is CU 12,000.
Additional profit before tax is CU 3,000.
A fall of more than CU 3,000 in project operating profit would eliminate the forecast gain although interest remains due.

questions.title: Section A · Willow Joinery
questions.stem: Willow is planning a small factory refit. Times are in working days. Activity A takes 4 days and B takes 6 days. Both can begin immediately. C takes 5 days after A. D takes 2 days after B. E takes 3 days and can start only after both C and D finish. All durations are deterministic for the initial plan.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the critical path and calculate the minimum project duration.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine total float on B and the effect of a two-day delay to B on overall completion.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain one reason the critical path could change during the refit.

steps.text: A–C ends after 9 days and B–D after 8.
The critical path is A–C–E.
Minimum duration is 12 working days.
The B–D branch has 1 day of float, so B has 1 day total float.
With the delay, B–D finishes at day 10 and E then takes 3.
Completion moves to day 13, a one-day project delay.
An uncertain activity duration could lengthen the currently shorter B–D branch beyond 9 days.
E would then wait for D, making that branch determine the completion date.

questions.title: Section B · Option 1 · Senna Lamps
questions.stem: Senna makes 12,000 lamps annually at CU 45 each. Operating profit is CU 54,000. Inventory averages CU 36,000, cost of sales CU 288,000 and trade payables CU 24,000. All CU 240,000 of annual purchases are on credit. Assume a 360-day year. A new supplier would deliver smaller batches, reducing average inventory to CU 24,000. Delivery charges of CU 4,800 a year would be new operating expenses. Units and cost of sales otherwise stay constant. The supplier has a single local depot.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate current inventory turnover in days.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate current creditor days and inventory days under the proposal.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the change in the operating profit margin and explain the difference between the cash released from inventory and this change in profit.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether Senna should adopt the new supply arrangement.

steps.text: $36000/288000$ multiplied by 360.
45 days.
$24000/240000$ multiplied by 360.
Creditor days are 36.
Divide the new inventory balance by the unchanged cost of sales and multiply by 360.
New inventory days are 30.
Revenue is CU 540,000 and margin falls from 10% to about 9.11%.
A decrease of about 0.89 percentage points.
CU 12,000 less average stock is a one-off release of working capital.
The delivery charge reduces annual operating profit by CU 4,800.

Fifteen fewer inventory days release cash and free storage, but the recurring CU 4,800 cost exceeds the one-off CU 12,000 release after two and a half years in a simple undiscounted comparison if no other savings arise. That comparison mixes a balance-sheet release with a recurring expense, so assess the opportunity cost of cash and space, service reliability and stockout risk. A second source or minimum buffer may make the switch feasible. A cash-constrained firm can reasonably place a higher value on the near-term release. Use best fit. Award 0 for no creditable response, 1–2 for limited assertions, 3–4 for a partially explained point with weak application, 5–6 for developed analysis using case evidence, 7–8 for supported consideration of competing arguments and a reasoned decision, and 9–10 for sustained evaluation integrating specific evidence, a material limitation and a convincing judgement. Credit a well-supported alternative.

questions.title: Section B · Option 2 · Fen Rail Events
questions.stem:
Fen chooses between a permanent venue and a portable stage. Both options have four-year lives and no scrap value. Net annual cash inflows, constant within each scenario, are shown below. Use a four-year annuity factor of 3.31. Each scenario applies for the full four years. The owner has limited access to borrowing. An outdoor portable stage can be hired at several sites.

| Option | Initial cost / CU | Annual inflow if busy / CU | Annual inflow if quiet / CU |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Venue | 180,000 | 80,000 | 35,000 |
| Stage | 100,000 | 45,000 | 32,000 |

The estimated probability of the busy scenario is 0.60.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the NPV of the venue in the busy scenario.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the probability-weighted expected NPV for each option.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate both quiet-scenario NPVs and explain how these outcomes inform a risk-averse owner.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Recommend an investment, taking account of both risk and the reliability of the figures.

steps.text: Venue expected annual inflow is CU 62,000.
Venue expected NPV is CU 25,220.
Stage expected annual inflow is CU 39,800.
Stage expected NPV is CU 31,738.
The stage stays positive in the modelled quiet case.
Limited borrowing makes the venue’s downside harder to absorb.

The stage gives CU 6,518 greater expected NPV at the stated probability and requires CU 80,000 less initial capital. The venue has a larger busy-case upside and may strengthen the brand through a fixed address. The probabilities rely on forecasts and the portable stage faces weather and site risks missing from the two-state model. Re-estimate demand, check venue financing and obtain site agreements. Select the stage if capital is tight or the quiet scenario is credible. A confidently higher probability of sustained busy trade can favour the venue. Use best fit. Award 0 for no creditable response, 1–2 for limited assertions, 3–4 for a partially explained point with weak application, 5–6 for developed analysis using case evidence, 7–8 for supported consideration of competing arguments and a reasoned decision, and 9–10 for sustained evaluation integrating specific evidence, a material limitation and a convincing judgement. Credit a well-supported alternative.
